passages.where: The woman sees that the tree is good for food, pleasing to the eyes and desirable for wisdom, and she takes and eats, and gives to her husband, who eats. The site's note says sin works through goods rightly made, food, beauty and wisdom all being God's gifts, and the wrong lies in seizing them against his word. The plain note says temptation begins with a question about God's goodness: is he holding out on you?

John warns against loving the world, which he describes as the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life, all passing away. The site's plain note says the world here means a way of life set against God, not God's good creation or the people in it, and that John's point is not letting appetite, envy or pride take God's place. It asks what you are building your life on that is passing away.

As the grave is never satisfied, so the eyes of man are never satisfied. The site's note on the chapter says it gathers sayings on the restless human appetite. The proverb sets the eye's hunger beside the grave's, one more thing that always has room for more.

The Teacher says all a person's labour is for the mouth, yet the appetite is never satisfied, and better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire. The site's note on the chapter says it describes a man who has riches, wealth and honor and cannot enjoy them, and that appetite is never satisfied. Having and enjoying are not the same thing.

Do not be amazed when someone grows rich and the splendour of his house increases, the psalm says, for he will carry nothing away. The site's plain note says the difference in this psalm is not between rich and poor, and asks whether you have understanding about what you own. Hold it, the note says, the way someone holds a thing they will have to leave.

Amos pictures the comfortable elite on ivory beds, eating the best lambs, drinking wine by the bowlful, and failing to grieve over the ruin of Joseph. The site's note says Amos is not condemning feasting, music or wine as such, which Scripture celebrates as God's gifts, but luxury gained through injustice and enjoyed in complacency. The chapter asks whether enjoyment has made a person unable to see or feel what is happening to others.

James tells rich landowners that their riches have rotted, their clothes are moth-eaten and their gold corroded, because they hoarded treasure. The site's note on the chapter says they hoarded wealth, withheld wages and condemned the innocent. The plain note asks how the people who make what you buy are paid.

Jesus says how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God, easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. The site's note says he does not call riches sinful but says they supply the security the kingdom asks a person to give up, and that the camel was a recognized way of speaking of the impossible, not a gate or a rope. The plain note asks what you trust to make you safe, and says the answer of verse 27 is for everyone: all things are possible with God.

Haggai tells the people that they eat but never have enough, put on clothes but never get warm, and earn wages to put into a bag with holes. The site's note on the chapter says they were living in panelled houses while the temple lay in ruins, and its hard note warns against turning this into a rule that every hardship has a simple spiritual cause. What carries over is the call to consider your ways.

Jesus tells his disciples not to worry about what they will eat or wear, for life is more than food and the body more than clothes. The site's note says the rich fool was anxious to secure too much and disciples may be anxious about securing enough, and both are answered by trust in the Father. The plain note says your heart follows your treasure: look where your money and time go, and you will see where your heart is.

misread.taken: I have come that they may have life in all its fullness is quoted as if Jesus promised a full life in the sense the advertisements mean: more comfort, more possessions, a better house and a better car.
misread.says: The site's note says the life Jesus gives is the eternal life of the whole Gospel, and its abundance is not wealth or comfort but fullness of relationship with God, given at the cost of the shepherd's own life. The plain note sets the verse against voices that come to take, your money, your loyalty, your time, and leave you emptier than they found you; Jesus says he came to give.

whole: Most people in rich countries do not feel rich. They feel behind. The phone is two years old, the kitchen looks tired next to a friend's, the children want what their classmates have, and every screen offers something that will make life easier, more beautiful or more like someone else's. Shopping can become a way to cope with a bad day, a reward for a hard week, or a way to feel in control. The cupboards fill, the storage units fill, the debt grows, and the satisfaction lasts about as long as the packaging. Many people know this and still cannot stop.

Scripture saw this long before advertising. Eve saw that the fruit was good for food, pleasing to the eye and desirable, and the site's note says sin works through goods rightly made by seizing them against God's word. Proverbs says the eyes of man are never satisfied, and the Teacher describes a man with riches and honor who cannot enjoy them, because appetite is never full. John names the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life, and says they are passing away. Underneath is the same question the serpent asked, whether God is holding out on us, and the same promise that the next thing will finally fill the gap. It never does. The site's note on Ecclesiastes 3 says God has set eternity in human hearts, and a heart with eternity in it is not filled by the next purchase.

So the Bible's wisdom does not despise good things. Amos condemned not feasting and music but luxury bought by injustice and enjoyed while others fell apart, and Jesus told his followers that life is more than food and the body more than clothes. In practice that means looking honestly at where the money and time go, since the heart follows them. It means asking, as James does, how the people who made what we buy are paid. It means enjoying what we have without needing the next thing, giving some of it away, and holding the rest the way the psalm says, like something we will have to leave. And it means noticing the bag with holes in it, the wages that never seem to stay, and considering our ways.

The hope Scripture gives is a fullness no shop can sell. Jesus came that his sheep might have life in all its fullness, and the note says that fullness is relationship with God, given at the cost of the shepherd's own life. Taste and see that the LORD is good, the psalm says; those who seek him lack no good thing. A person who has tasted that can walk past the window without needing what is in it.
sit: What did you last buy hoping it would make you feel better, and what were you really hoping for?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says taste and see is an invitation, not an argument: you cannot know a food by reading about it, and the psalm asks you to try trusting God and find out.
